opus-5.5.text:
I think the delta rule itself was never the problem. The idea is quite old: it goes back to Widrow and Hoff, and Schmidhuber's group connected it to fast weight programmers years ago. People knew that, compared with plain linear attention, the delta rule gives you a much better memory update. Instead of just adding key-value associations into the state, you first look at what the memory currently retrieves for that key and correct the error. Linear attention keeps piling things on and the memory gets polluted. The delta rule can actually overwrite.

The issue was training efficiency. The delta rule update is inherently sequential: each step's state depends on the previous one in a way that isn't a simple elementwise decay. So people trained it with a recurrent loop over time, which is terrible for GPUs. You can't use tensor cores well, you can't scale to long sequences or big models, and so it stayed a nice idea that nobody could train at the scale of a modern language model.

What our work did was show that you can parallelize it over sequence length. The key observation is that the delta rule's transition is a generalized Householder transformation, so a product of those across a chunk can be written compactly with the WY representation from numerical linear algebra. That's a classic trick people used for things like QR decomposition. With that, you can do chunkwise parallel training like we did for gated linear attention: within a chunk you do dense matrix multiplications that run well on tensor cores, and across chunks you only pass the state recurrently. The sequential part shrinks from the sequence length to the number of chunks, and most of the computation becomes matmuls.

So I'd say the algorithm turned DeltaNet from something theoretically appealing into something you can actually train at billions of parameters on lots of tokens, and compare fairly against Transformers and Mamba. Once it was practical, people could see empirically that the delta rule really helps, especially on recall-intensive tasks. That opened the door to follow-ups like Gated DeltaNet, which combines the delta rule with gating, and now variants show up in fairly large production models.

More broadly, the lesson for me is that in architecture research, hardware efficiency isn't an afterthought. An idea that can't be mapped onto matmuls effectively doesn't exist at scale. A lot of my work has been finding the right algebraic structure so that an expressive recurrence becomes hardware-friendly. Often the math is already sitting in an old numerical linear algebra textbook; you just have to recognize it.

r001.rationale: The response says the algorithm parallelizes DeltaNet across sequence chunks, shifts most computation to tensor-core-friendly matrix multiplications, and makes the model practical to train at scale.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the algorithm’s role in Delta-Ro’s development with FlashAttention’s role in sparse attention’s development.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the algorithm didn't invent anything about DeltaNet conceptually. The delta rule itself goes back decades, and Imanol Schlag and Jürgen Schmidhuber had already shown in 2021 that it fixes a real problem with linear attention, which is that a plain additive update can only write into memory and never erase. Their DeltaNet could actually overwrite old associations. The modeling story was already there.

The problem was that nobody could train it at scale. The update is inherently recurrent: the new state depends on the old state in a way that isn't just a sum, so you couldn't use the chunkwise parallel tricks people had for ordinary linear attention. You were stuck with a sequential loop over tokens, and on a GPU that's just death. So DeltaNet sat there as a nice idea that lost to things like Mamba and GLA simply because it couldn't be trained fast.

What we noticed is that each delta update is essentially a generalized Householder transformation on the state. And there's a very old piece of numerical linear algebra, the WY representation, that lets you compress a product of Householder matrices into a compact form that can be applied with matrix multiplications instead of a chain of dependent steps. Once you see that, the chunkwise algorithm almost writes itself. Within a chunk you do a small amount of sequential work to build the compact representation, and then everything across chunks and across the hidden dimension becomes matmuls, which is exactly what tensor cores want.

So the way I'd describe my role is that I made the economics work. The algorithm turned DeltaNet from something that trained an order of magnitude slower than its competitors into something that runs at roughly the speed of GLA. That's the difference between a paper that gets cited as an interesting ablation and a model family that people actually build on. And I think the bigger lesson I took from it is that a lot of ideas in sequence modeling aren't dead because they're wrong, they're dead because someone hasn't found the right way to map them onto hardware yet. The modeling and the kernel really have to be designed together.

r001.rationale: The response says Yang’s chunkwise algorithm replaces dependent updates with matrix multiplications suited to tensor cores, making DeltaNet run roughly as fast as GLA.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the algorithm’s role to FlashAttention’s role in sparse attention’s development.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame its role as closing the gap between an algorithm that works in principle and one that is useful in practice. You can have a promising method, but if it takes too long to run, it limits both experimentation and deployment.

The point of parallelization is to expose work that can happen simultaneously without letting communication and synchronization consume the benefit. So the contribution isn’t simply “use more processors.” It’s organizing the computation so that additional hardware actually helps.

That’s how I’d understand its role in making Delta-Ro practical: reducing the computational barrier so that the underlying method can be explored and used. It’s an enabling piece, rather than the whole story.

r001.rationale: It says the parallelization organizes computation so added hardware helps and reduces the computational barrier to using Delta-Ro, conveying efficient implementation on hardware.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the algorithm’s role to FlashAttention’s role in sparse attention’s development.

sol-6.1.text: I see the parallel algorithm as the bridge between the idea and an implementation you can actually use. A method can have attractive properties on paper, but if its computation is too sequential, it becomes difficult to run efficiently at scale. My contribution was to expose the parallelism in that computation so it could make better use of the hardware. That was an important part of making Delta-Ro practical, alongside the design of the method itself.

r001.rationale: The response says Yang exposed parallelism so Delta-Ro could use hardware more effectively and become practical to run at scale.
